title: Steady Under Pressure
tagline: Twelve short sessions on steadiness: the surge, early cues, six seconds, the exhale, the step away, naming it, the short apology, and steady habits.
course_purpose: Twelve short film sessions on steadiness: the surge, early cues, six seconds, the exhale, the step away, naming it, the short apology, and the habits underneath. Consistency, trained where you stand.
audience: For every man, on either track. Steadiness skills for pressure at home, work, and in program life. Not anger management, batterer intervention, or a substitute for any court-mandated program.
facilitator_note: Self-paced film. About twelve minutes each. Watch when you can. A Certified Facilitator is available for questions and accountability when your seat is claimed. Optional live cohorts may be offered by some programs. Every drill except a live home repair is practicable wherever you are right now. Logged sessions and a checkable practice. Completion never requires contact with your child, and no practice ever asks you to go beyond the rules that govern you now or any court order. Not anger management, batterer intervention, or a substitute for any court-mandated program; not designed or validated for those purposes and never ordered in their place.

sessions.title: The Surge Is a Signal
sessions.keyline: The surge is a signal, not an order.
sessions.one_scene: The noise in the meal line rises, trays and voices. His jaw sets before he knows why. That jaw is the earliest cue, and it is not an order to blow.
sessions.in_the_room: The body's stress response in plain language. You learn that the surge fires before deliberation, and that the skill is what you do in the next few seconds.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can treat the surge as information instead of a command.
sessions.practice: Log three moments of rising tension this week. For each, write the trigger and the earliest body cue you noticed.
sessions.science_or_note: The surge chemistry of stress fires before awareness; early cues give you a choice.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why does the surge arrive faster than your thinking?

sessions.title: Know Your Early Cues
sessions.keyline: Catch it in the jaw, not the shout.
sessions.one_scene: He used to notice only when his voice was already loud. Now he catches the heat in his face and the locked jaw two beats earlier. That gap is the whole game.
sessions.in_the_room: You map your personal early warning signs: jaw, fists, breath, tone, tunnel vision. You pick the two that show up first for you.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can name your earliest cues before the shout arrives.
sessions.practice: Write your top two early cues on a card. Check the card after three hard moments this week.
sessions.science_or_note: Body cues precede peak anger; naming them early widens the window to choose.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Where does this session tell you to catch the surge?
choices: In the shout

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why name your early cues in writing?

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which is an early cue, as this session means it?
choices: A long rant

Leaving the house for the night

sessions.title: Six Seconds
sessions.keyline: Six seconds buy your judgment back.
sessions.one_scene: The words are already loaded. He counts six silent seconds instead. The sentence he almost said stays unsaid, and the one he says next is his.
sessions.in_the_room: What happens in the seconds before a blowup, including the fast pathway that outruns judgment. The tool is a deliberate pause of about six seconds before you speak or act.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can insert six seconds when you feel the surge.
sessions.practice: Practice a six-second pause three times this week in real moments. Record the trigger and what you did after the pause.
sessions.science_or_note: A brief pause brings judgment back online after the fast threat pathway fires.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What do six seconds buy you, per this session?
choices: Your judgment back
The other person's apology
The end of the feeling

checkpoint_questions.prompt: When is the six-second pause practiced so it works under load?
choices: Only in real conflict
In the boring hours, daily, so it is there when the surge comes
Once at the start of the course

checkpoint_questions.prompt: You feel the surge mid-conversation. Which is the session's move?
choices: Push through so they know you care
Take six silent seconds before you speak
End the conversation for the night

script_aids.purpose: Install a six-second pause that buys judgment back under pressure.
script_aids.practical_insight: Six seconds buy your judgment back.

sessions.title: The Long Exhale
sessions.keyline: A long exhale stands the body down.
sessions.one_scene: His chest is high and tight. He lengthens the out-breath once, slow. The shoulders drop a notch. He can hear himself think again.
sessions.in_the_room: Slow breathing with a longer exhale as a body-down tool you can run anywhere. You pair it with the six-second pause so the skill stacks.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can lower your own charge on demand with one long exhale.
sessions.practice: Run a daily long-exhale drill for five days. Use it once live under pressure and note what changed.
sessions.science_or_note: A long slow exhale signals the body to stand down faster than willpower alone.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why the long exhale specifically?
choices: It looks calm to others
A long slow exhale stands the body down faster than willpower does
It gives you something to count

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What is the drill this session asks you to own?
choices: Hold your breath until the feeling passes
A daily long-exhale practice you can run anywhere
A loud sigh in front of the other person

checkpoint_questions.prompt: The surge hits and you already took six seconds. What next?
choices: Argue harder with a clear head
Run one long slow exhale to stand the body down
Skip the exhale if you already paused

script_aids.purpose: Pair the pause with a long exhale that stands the body down on demand.

sessions.title: Step Away to Come Back
sessions.one_scene: Mid-argument on a call, his voice is climbing. He says he needs ten minutes and that he is coming back. He does, on time, quieter. The coming back is the skill.
sessions.in_the_room: Using a time-out on yourself as a reset, not a punishment. You practice leaving without abandoning the person or the topic.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can step away to cool down and return on time.
sessions.practice: Take one clean self time-out during a hard moment where you are now, then return when you said. Report both ends.
sessions.science_or_note: A clean break lets the body reset; the return keeps it from becoming abandonment.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What is the purpose of stepping away in this session?
choices: To win the argument by leaving
To come back; the step away serves the return
To show how upset you are

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What makes a step away different from storming out?
choices: Volume
Saying where you are going and when you are coming back
Nothing; they are the same

checkpoint_questions.prompt: You feel yourself flooding mid-conversation with your child. Which is the session's move?
choices: Push through so they know you care
Name it, step out briefly, return when you said
End the conversation for the night

script_aids.purpose: Train stepping away as a reset that still returns on time.

sessions.title: The Line You Leave On
sessions.keyline: Say the line, then leave the room.
sessions.one_scene: He almost storms out silent. Instead he says: I need ten minutes. I am coming back. Then he leaves. The room stays safer because the line held the door open.
sessions.in_the_room: You write and rehearse a short leave-line that names the break and the return time. No speech. No blame. Just the line, then the exit.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You have a leave-line ready so a break is a reset, not a disappearance.
sessions.practice: Write your leave-line in under fifteen words. Rehearse it aloud three times. Use it once this week if needed.
sessions.science_or_note: Naming the return turns a break into a trustworthy pause.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What belongs in the line you leave on?
choices: A long explanation of why you are right
A short line that names the break and when you return
Silence, then disappear

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why say the line before you leave the room?
choices: So the other person feels guilty
So the break is a reset, not abandonment
So you win the argument

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which line fits this session?
choices: I need ten minutes. I am coming back.
Forget it. I am done talking.
You always do this.

script_aids.purpose: Give him a short leave-line so a break is a trustworthy pause, not a disappearance.
script_aids.practical_insight: Say the line, then leave the room.

sessions.title: Name the Feeling
sessions.keyline: Say the feeling so you do not have to show it.
sessions.one_scene: Instead of the slammed cabinet, he says I am frustrated, and not at you. Five words. The temperature drops a degree, and the child hears the words too.
sessions.in_the_room: Putting feelings into words lowers their intensity. You practice naming your own state in plain language before it becomes a show.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can handle feelings by naming them instead of acting them out.
sessions.practice: Name one feeling out loud in three separate moments this week. Log the words you used.
sessions.science_or_note: Naming a feeling out loud measurably lowers its charge.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why does saying the feeling out loud matter, per this session?
choices: So you do not have to show it instead
So others feel responsible for it
It does not; feelings should stay private

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which sentence is naming it, as this session teaches?
choices: You are making me angry.
I am angry right now, and I need a minute before we keep going.
Everyone needs to calm down.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What does a child learn from a father who names his anger plainly?
choices: That anger is shameful
That big feelings can be handled with words
That the father is weak

script_aids.purpose: Teach naming the feeling so the body does not have to show it as damage.
script_aids.practical_insight: Say the feeling so you do not have to show it.

sessions.title: Feelings Without Weapons
sessions.one_scene: He almost says you always do this. He swaps it for I am angry and I want to finish this calmly. Same feeling. No weapon attached.
sessions.in_the_room: You strip blame, insults, and history dumps from the naming sentence. Clean naming lowers heat; loaded naming restarts the fight.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can name hard feelings without arming them.
sessions.practice: Rewrite two loaded sentences into clean feeling statements. Use one clean line live this week.
sessions.science_or_note: Blame reloads conflict; clean labeling keeps the skill usable.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What does 'without loading it' mean here?
choices: Never feel anger
Name the feeling without blame, insults, or history dumps
Only write feelings, never say them

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which line names the feeling without a weapon?
choices: I am frustrated, and I want to finish this calmly.
You always ruin everything when I am tired.
Fine. Whatever.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why strip the weapon from the sentence?
choices: Because feelings are wrong
Because blame reloads the fight; clean naming lowers heat
Because the other person should guess

script_aids.purpose: Separate feeling from weaponized behavior; feelings are allowed, weapons are not.
script_aids.emotional_beat: Recognition that leads to a concrete next move.

sessions.title: Own It Same Day
sessions.keyline: Own it out loud, same day.
sessions.one_scene: Last night he barked over nothing. This morning, before anything else: I was wrong to raise my voice. You did not deserve that. Same day. No wait.
sessions.in_the_room: Repair after a rupture protects the relationship. You practice owning the moment out loud the same day, specific and without excuses.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can own a bad moment the same day it happened.
sessions.practice: Write one ownership line for a recent miss. Deliver it same day if contact is allowed, or deliver a live ownership to someone where you are now.
sessions.science_or_note: Fast ownership keeps a rupture from hardening into the relationship's normal.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What is the standard for owning it, per this session?
choices: Out loud, same day, without excuses
A general apology when things are calm next week
Letting actions speak over time

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why same day instead of waiting?
choices: Children have short memories
Fast ownership keeps the rupture from hardening into the relationship's normal
It gets the discomfort over with

checkpoint_questions.prompt: You barked last night and morning is here. The move is?
choices: Wait until they bring it up
Own it out loud today, specific and without defense
Do something fun and move on

script_aids.purpose: Require same-day ownership after a miss so rupture does not harden overnight.
script_aids.practical_insight: Own it out loud, same day.

sessions.title: The Short Apology
sessions.one_scene: He starts to explain the week. He stops. He says only: I raised my voice at you. That was wrong. I will step away next time. Ten words. It lands.
sessions.in_the_room: You practice a short apology script: the specific act, that it was wrong, and one next step. Defense stays out.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can apologize short, specific, and without defense.
sessions.practice: Write a short apology for one real miss. Cut every excuse. Rehearse once aloud, then deliver if allowed.
sessions.science_or_note: Short specific repair lands; defense undoes it.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which of these is a repair and not an excuse?
choices: I was tired; you know how my week was.
I raised my voice at you. That was wrong, and it is mine to fix.
I am sorry you got upset.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What stays out of the short apology?
choices: The specific thing you did
Defense, blame, and a long story
A plan for next time

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why keep the apology short?
choices: So you can leave faster
Short and specific lands; defense undoes it
Children prefer vague words

sessions.title: Sleep, Food, Movement
sessions.keyline: Steadiness is built in the boring hours.
sessions.one_scene: Lights out at the same hour five nights straight, a walk or a workout most days, and by day five the fuse is longer. He can see it in his own log.
sessions.in_the_room: The daily regulators that raise your threshold: sleep, food, and movement. Willpower sits on top of a body that is fed and rested.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You can lower baseline reactivity through habits practicable anywhere.
sessions.practice: Hold one sleep anchor and one movement block for five days. Note food timing on the same log.
sessions.science_or_note: Sleep, food, and movement raise the threshold where steadiness breaks.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Where does this session say steadiness is actually built?
choices: In dramatic moments of self-control
In the boring hours: sleep, food, movement
In willpower alone

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Why do sleep and routine belong in this course?
choices: They are filler
A depleted body fires the alarm sooner and louder; the habits raise your threshold
They replace the need for the pause

checkpoint_questions.prompt: Which weekly marker fits this session?
choices: Never feel the surge again
Lights out by a set hour five nights, plus one movement block most days
A promise to avoid hard conversations

script_aids.purpose: Ground steadiness in sleep, food, and movement so the body is not always one spark from fire.

sessions.title: Your Steady Week
sessions.keyline: Stack the small things until they hold.
sessions.one_scene: Nothing dramatic happened this week. He ran the pause, the leave-line, the short apology, and the sleep anchor. That is what holding looks like from inside.
sessions.in_the_room: You fold the course into a one-page steady week: cues, six seconds, exhale, leave-line, same-day ownership, and two boring-hour anchors.
sessions.what_you_leave_with: You leave with a written steady-week plan and one measurable marker.
sessions.practice: Complete a one-page steady-week plan with one weekly marker you will report to your facilitator or accountability partner.
sessions.science_or_note: Small repeated anchors outperform rare heroic effort.

checkpoint_questions.prompt: What does this course ask you to leave with?
choices: A promise to never feel the surge again
A trained pause, a named feeling, a fast repair, and daily habits that hold them up
A list of people who provoke you

checkpoint_questions.prompt: How do you stack a steady week?
choices: One big heroic day
Small anchors repeated until they hold
Waiting until life is less busy

checkpoint_questions.prompt: The line of this session is?
choices: Stack the small things until they hold.
White-knuckle every moment.
Skip the boring hours.
